questions.story:
On a Piece of Chalk
Adapted from a lecture by T. H. Huxley, 1868

Passage 1
If a well were sunk at our feet in the midst of the city of Norwich, the diggers would very soon find themselves at work in that white substance almost too soft to be called rock, with which we are all familiar as chalk. Not only here, but over the whole county and far beyond it, this same bed lies beneath the soil. It is, therefore, no trifling matter.

Passage 2
The chalk extends under the greater part of England and crosses the Channel into France and Germany. Moreover, borings have proved it to lie, in places, more than a thousand feet in thickness. These are not conjectures. They are measurements, taken carefully, and any man who doubts them may go and take them again for himself.

Passage 3
Place the smallest fragment under a microscope, however, and the apparently homogeneous mass resolves itself into a multitude of minute bodies. Each is the shell of a creature so infinitesimal that a thousand might rest upon a pin’s head. The chalk, in short, is not stone at all. It is a cemetery, and every grain of it was once alive.

Passage 4
Now, these creatures live only in the depths of the sea. Consequently, the ground upon which this hall is built was once the floor of an ocean. I am aware that the statement sounds extravagant; nevertheless, it follows necessarily from the evidence, and no other explanation accounts for what the microscope plainly shows.

Passage 5
How long, then, did the making of this bed require? The creatures fall slowly, and a thousand feet of them is a prodigious accumulation. Reckon it as you please: the answer runs into millions of years. Some will find that figure unwelcome. But the chalk is indifferent to our preferences, and it lies there whether we are willing to read it or not.

Passage 6
I have taken this humble stone, therefore, and asked it a few questions. It has answered them. A man who learns to interrogate the commonest object at his feet has acquired the whole method of science, and he needs no laboratory and no learning beyond attention. That, gentlemen, is within the reach of every one of you.
